name: Process-Level Eval
question: Where exactly did it go wrong?
summary: Open the black box and score the trajectory: the plan, each tool call and its arguments, the order of steps, and how the agent recovered from errors. It turns a failed run into a specific fix.
useCases: Debugging failures that system-level eval surfaced
Tuning tool descriptions, prompts and planning logic
Catching agents that succeed wastefully through loops or redundant calls

items.detail: right tool chosen at each step
exact, in-order or any-order vs a reference path
failed calls the agent retried or routed around
executed steps that follow the stated plan

steps: Instrument the agent so every step is a trace span (OpenTelemetry works well)
Define reference trajectories for key tasks, or a per-step rubric
Score each step with code checks first, then an LLM judge for judgment calls
Aggregate by step type to find the weakest link
pitfalls: Many paths can be valid, and exact-match scoring punishes good alternatives
Reference trajectories are costly to write and go stale when tools change
Step scores can look fine while the final outcome still fails
remember: Grade the path, not just the destination.
caption: Each step gets its own verdict, so the failure has an exact location.

comparison.needs: Traces + reference path or step rubric

steps.title: Capture the trace
steps.text: Instrument the agent so every tool call becomes a span with its name, arguments, result and error.

steps.title: Write the reference path
steps.text: For key tasks, record the steps a correct run needs: find the order, fetch the account, issue the refund.

steps.title: Match the trajectory
steps.text: Exact match fails because of an extra call. In-order match passes: the reference steps appear in order.

steps.title: Measure efficiency
steps.text: 3 needed steps ÷ 4 actual = 0.75. The repeated get_account is waste, often caused by a vague tool description.

steps.title: Check the arguments
steps.text: issue_refund was called with USD instead of INR. The outcome might still look fine, but this step is wrong.

steps.title: Report per step
steps.text: Aggregate findings by tool across many traces. Fix the weakest tool first.

pros: Pinpoints the exact step that went wrong
Catches wasteful or risky intermediate actions even when the outcome passes
Turns failures into specific prompt and tool fixes
Scores failed runs usefully, not just as zeros
cons: Reference paths are costly to write and go stale
Strict matching penalizes valid alternative paths
Good step scores don’t guarantee a good outcome
avoidWhen: Tools and flows are still changing daily (references go stale)
Many equally valid paths exist and you have no step rubric

playgroundGuide.scenario: A refund agent should do three things in order: find the order, fetch the customer's account, then issue the refund in INR. You're looking at the trace of what it actually did, one tool call per chip, and scoring each step against that reference.
controls: Click a + button to add that tool call to the end of the trajectory.
Undo removes the last call; Reset restores the starting trace.
Choose the currency the agent passed to issue_refund.

outputs.name: Exact match
outputs.meaning: Identical to the reference: same steps, same order, nothing extra.

outputs.name: In-order match
outputs.meaning: The reference steps appear in the right order; extra steps are allowed.

outputs.name: Any-order match
outputs.meaning: Every reference step appears somewhere, in any order.

outputs.name: Step efficiency
outputs.meaning: Needed steps ÷ steps taken. 100% means no wasted calls.

outputs.name: Arguments correct
outputs.meaning: issue_refund used INR, the currency this business settles in.

presets.name: Starting trace
presets.expect: One repeated call and the wrong currency: exact match fails, in-order passes, efficiency 75%.

presets.name: Perfect run
presets.expect: Exactly the reference with INR. Every check passes and efficiency is 100%.

presets.name: Wasteful but correct
presets.expect: Right order and currency, plus two extra calls. In-order passes, exact fails, efficiency 60%.

presets.name: Wrong order
presets.expect: Fetches the account before finding the order. In-order fails, but any-order still passes.

missions.text: Get an exact match with correct arguments.
missions.hint: Reset, remove the extra call, and pick INR.

goals: Distinguish exact, in-order and any-order trajectory matching
Calculate step efficiency and spot redundant calls
Explain how step-level scores turn a failure into a specific fix

practice.scenario: A payout-reconciliation agent keeps calling get_account twice and sometimes sends the wrong currency to issue_refund. Scoring 80 traced runs step by step shows the argument errors cluster in one tool whose description was ambiguous. Rewriting that description fixes most failures before anyone touches the model.

industries.use: Audit reconciliation agents for the right tool and arguments at each step
Check prior-authorization agents follow the required step order
Score incident agents on checking logs before restarting services

practice.analogy: A maths exam that gives marks for working. Even when the final answer is wrong, you can see exactly which line went wrong.

samples.code:
reference = ["find_order", "get_account", "issue_refund"]
actual = [
    ("find_order", {"id": "8812"}),
    ("get_account",   {"id": "A7"}),
    ("get_account",   {"id": "A7"}),                  # redundant repeat
    ("issue_refund",  {"amount": 499, "cur": "USD"}), # wrong currency
]
tools = [name for name, _ in actual]

def in_order_match(ref, got):
    it = iter(got)
    return all(step in it for step in ref)   # ref appears in order, extras allowed

exact      = tools == reference
in_order   = in_order_match(reference, tools)
efficiency = len(reference) / len(tools)
bad_args   = [a for n, a in actual if n == "issue_refund" and a["cur"] != "INR"]

print(exact, in_order, round(efficiency, 2), bad_args)
# False True 0.75 [{'amount': 499, 'cur': 'USD'}]

numericDrill.question: Reference path: [search, get_account, refund]. Actual: [search, get_account, get_account, lookup_fx, refund]. What is the step efficiency? Does the in-order match pass?
numericDrill.answer: Efficiency = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6. The in-order match passes because search, get_account and refund appear in that order with extra steps allowed. An exact match fails.

interview.question: What's the difference between exact, in-order and any-order trajectory matching?
interview.answer: Exact requires the same tool sequence. In-order requires the reference steps to appear in order but allows extra steps. Any-order only requires every reference step to appear somewhere. Stricter matching penalizes valid alternatives, so choose per task.

interview.question: How would you debug an agent that succeeds but costs 3× more than expected?
interview.answer: Trace every step, then look at step efficiency and redundant calls per tool. The cause is usually a vague tool description, missing information in a tool result, or no clear stop condition, and each shows up in process-level scores.

mistakes.mistake: Requiring an exact match to one reference path
mistakes.fix: Use in-order or any-order matching, or a per-step rubric

mistakes.mistake: Logging tool names without arguments and results
mistakes.fix: Trace arguments and results for every span

quiz.question: A reconciliation agent issued the correct refund but called get_account three times. Which technique flags this?
quiz.explanation: The outcome is fine, but the path is wasteful. Step efficiency catches it.

quiz.question: Reference path: [find_order, get_account, issue_refund]. Actual: [find_order, lookup_fx, get_account, issue_refund]. Which matches pass?
quiz.explanation: The extra lookup_fx breaks exact match, but the reference steps still appear in order.

quiz.question: Reference: [check_stock, reserve_item, send_confirmation]. Actual: [reserve_item, check_stock, send_confirmation]. Which match passes?
quiz.explanation: All steps are present, but not in order, so only any-order passes. Reserving before checking stock is a real bug.

quiz.question: What should each trace span record so steps can be scored? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Name, arguments and result are what you score. Never log secrets or card numbers.

quiz.question: A plan-change task needs 4 steps. The agent took 10. What is the step efficiency?
quiz.explanation: Needed ÷ taken = 4 ÷ 10 = 0.4.

quiz.question: The agent keeps calling the same lookup tool again and again. Which are likely causes? Select all that apply.
options: The tool result is missing information the agent needs
quiz.explanation: All three leave the agent re-checking. Temperature is rarely the root cause; fix the tool description, the result and the stop condition first.

quiz.question: A legal-research agent can reach a good memo by many different search paths. What is the best way to score its steps?
options: Exact match to one reference path
A per-step rubric scored by an LLM judge
quiz.explanation: A rubric judges whether each step was sensible without demanding one fixed path.

quiz.question: A transfer agent must complete a KYC check before moving money. Which check enforces this?
options: A precedence check: check_kyc must come before any transfer call
quiz.explanation: Order matters here. A plain in-order match would still pass [transfer, check_kyc, transfer], so check that no transfer happens before KYC.

quiz.question: Step scores look perfect, but claims tasks still fail. What is the likely explanation?
options: The step checks miss what the outcome needs, so run system-level eval too
quiz.explanation: Good steps do not guarantee a good outcome. Use both levels.

quiz.question: Your team needs to capture agent traces for step scoring. Which tools fit? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: BM25 is a keyword-ranking function, not a tracing tool.

quiz.question: In 6% of runs, issue_refund is called with cur="USD" for an INR account. The outcome check still reads “refund issued”. What catches this?
options: An argument check on that step: currency must match the account
quiz.explanation: Argument-level checks catch wrong inputs that a status-only outcome check misses.

quiz.question: In 80 failed traces, 70% of the argument errors come from one tool whose description is ambiguous. What is the best first fix?
options: Rewrite that tool’s description and parameter schema, then re-run
quiz.explanation: Clustered errors point to the tool interface. Fix it before touching the model.

quiz.question: A claims agent must never call submit_claim before get_eligibility. How should a violation count?
options: As a hard fail, even if the final outcome looks right
Ignore it if the claim went through
Only when step efficiency is low
quiz.explanation: Safety or compliance ordering rules are pass/fail. A good outcome does not excuse them.

quiz.question: A shopping agent calls search_products 25 times until it hits the step limit. Which check flags it?
quiz.explanation: Loop detection and step efficiency flag this. The fix is usually a clear stop condition.

quiz.question: Which are useful argument-level checks for file_claim? Select all that apply.
options: claim_id matches the one in the customer’s message
amount is within the policy limit
The argument JSON is neatly indented
quiz.explanation: Check that arguments are correct for this customer and policy. Formatting does not matter.

quiz.question: You collect 20,000 agent traces a day. How do you apply process-level eval affordably?
options: Have an LLM judge score every trace
Run cheap code checks on all traces and send a sample to an LLM rubric
Review traces only when customers complain
quiz.explanation: Code checks scale to every trace. Spend judge calls on a sample and on flagged traces.

quiz.question: An incident agent must read logs before restarting a service. It restarted first, then read the logs, and the incident was resolved. How should this be scored?
options: Flag it: the required order was broken, even though the outcome was fine
Pass, with a note for the user
quiz.explanation: Next time, restarting blind could destroy evidence or worsen an outage. Process rules exist for exactly this.

quiz.question: Exact-path match fails on 60% of runs while 90% of outcomes pass. What is the most likely reason?
options: Exact match is too strict because several paths are valid; use in-order match or a rubric
quiz.explanation: Exact match only suits tasks with one right path.

quiz.question: Success rate dropped from 91% to 84% after a tool update. What is the fastest way to find out why?
options: Group the failed traces by their first failing step
quiz.explanation: Grouping by first failing step points straight at what broke.

quiz.question: A fare-search tool returns “rate_limited”, and the agent retries immediately eight times before it succeeds. What should process eval report?
options: Retries without backoff, counted as redundant steps and poor error handling
quiz.explanation: Error handling is part of the path. Immediate retries waste cost and can worsen rate limits.
